title: Dates, versions and IP addresses
summary: A regex checks the shape, a parser checks the meaning: ISO 8601 dates with TryParseExact, semantic versions by the semver.org rules, and IPv4 addresses that IPAddress.TryParse alone would let through.

steps.title: Shape first, meaning second
body: This pattern finds ISO 8601 dates (`yyyy-MM-dd`) and already refuses month 13 and day 32. But look at the second
line: `2026-02-30` matches. February's length depends on the month and on leap years. A regex *could* encode that,
and the result would be unreadable and still wrong in some corner.
So split the job:
1. A regex **finds candidates** with the right shape.
2. A parser **validates** them: `DateTime.TryParseExact(s, "yyyy-MM-dd", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None, out var d)`,
or `DateOnly.TryParseExact` for a date without a time.
Always pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` for machine formats. With the current culture, a server set to `th-TH`
uses the Buddhist calendar (year 2569), and other cultures change separators. For timestamps with an offset, parse
with `DateTimeOffset.TryParseExact(s, "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:sszzz", ...)` or the round-trip format `"O"`.
One more habit: write `[0-9]`, not `\d`. In .NET, `\d` also matches other scripts' digits such as `٢`.

steps.explain: February 30 never exists. 2028 is a leap year. 2100 is not: years divisible by 100 are leap years only when also divisible by 400. That is exactly the kind of rule you do not want to write as a regex.

steps.title: Symptom: month 13 got into the bookings table
prompt: **Symptom.** The bookings import validates dates with `\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}`. This morning a row with `2026-13-45`
reached the database, and a support ticket shows a date typed with Arabic-Indic digits that crashed the billing job.
Tighten the shape: four ASCII digits, a month `01` to `12`, a day `01` to `31`. (`2026-02-31` still has a valid
shape; the next step deals with it.)
hints: Month: either `0` followed by 1 to 9, or `1` followed by 0 to 2. Day: `0[1-9]`, `[12][0-9]` or `3[01]`.
steps.explain: Alternation per field keeps each range readable. `[0-9]` instead of `\d` rejects other scripts' digits, which .NET's `\d` accepts unless you use `RegexOptions.ECMAScript`.

steps.title: Symptom: the report listed 2026-02-31
prompt: **Symptom.** The nightly report pulls booking dates out of free-text notes. Yesterday it listed `2026-02-31`, and the
billing job that reads the report crashed on it. It also picked `2026-11-26` out of the reference `12026-11-26`.
Fix `List<string> ValidDates(string text)`. It returns every `yyyy-MM-dd` date in `text` that is a **real calendar
date**, in order of appearance:
- Find candidates with ASCII digits only, and not as part of a longer run of digits: use `(?<![0-9])` before and
`(?![0-9])` after. (`\b` would fail on `2026-11-26T09:12`, because `6` and `T` are both word characters.)
- Keep a candidate only if `DateOnly.TryParseExact(value, "yyyy-MM-dd", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None, out _)`
succeeds.
`System.Text.RegularExpressions` and `System.Globalization` are imported.
template: using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using System.Globalization;
{{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("keeps real dates, drops February 31", new List<string> { "2026-11-26", "2028-02-29" }, ValidDates("check-in 2026-11-26, check-out 2026-02-31, rebooked 2028-02-29"));
Dojo.Eq("finds the date part of a timestamp", new List<string> { "2026-11-26" }, ValidDates("ts=2026-11-26T09:12:04Z"));
Dojo.Eq("ignores a date inside a longer number", new List<string>(), ValidDates("ref 12026-11-26"));
Dojo.Eq("2026 is not a leap year", new List<string>(), ValidDates("due 2026-02-29"));
Dojo.Eq("no dates in plain text", new List<string>(), ValidDates("call me tomorrow"));
hints: Change the pattern to `(?<![0-9])[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}(?![0-9])`, then filter with `TryParseExact`.

steps.title: Semantic versions, by the spec
body: Package versions follow **Semantic Versioning 2.0.0** (semver.org): `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, an optional pre-release
after `-`, and optional build metadata after `+`:
```text
The rules people get wrong:
- Numbers have **no leading zeros**: `1.02.0` is invalid. So each number is `0|[1-9][0-9]*`, not `[0-9]+`.
- Pre-release and build parts are dot-separated identifiers of `[0-9A-Za-z-]`. Empty identifiers are invalid: `1.0.0-`
- Build metadata is ignored when comparing versions.
semver.org publishes an official regex that also forbids leading zeros in numeric pre-release identifiers. Below is
the core of it. In production .NET code, `NuGet.Versioning`'s `SemanticVersion.TryParse` does the parsing and the
comparing for you.

steps.title: Validate a semantic version
prompt: The release pipeline must refuse a tag that is not a valid semantic version. Write a pattern that matches a whole
version with the named groups `major`, `minor`, `patch`, and optional `pre` (after `-`) and `build` (after `+`).
Numbers: `0` or a digit 1-9 followed by digits. Pre-release and build: one or more identifiers of `[0-9A-Za-z-]`,
separated by single dots. The `-` and `+` are not part of the groups.
hints: Each number is `(?<major>0|[1-9][0-9]*)`. An identifier list is `[0-9A-Za-z-]+(?:\.[0-9A-Za-z-]+)*`.
Make the tails optional and keep the sign outside the group: `(?:-(?<pre>...))?(?:\+(?<build>...))?`
steps.explain: The alternation `0|[1-9][0-9]*` is how specs say "no leading zeros". The same idea appears in JSON numbers and in IPv4 octets, next.

steps.prompt: A firewall admin page validates the IPv4 address a user types with `IPAddress.TryParse(input, out _)` alone. What goes wrong?
options: It accepts legacy forms: `1` becomes 0.0.0.1, `0x7f.1` becomes 127.0.0.1 and `010.0.0.1` becomes 8.0.0.1, so a rule can target a different host than the user meant
It rejects addresses with a zero octet, such as 10.0.0.1
It throws a FormatException on invalid input
Nothing: TryParse is a strict validator for dotted IPv4
steps.explain: `IPAddress.TryParse` follows the old BSD `inet_aton` rules: one to four parts, hex with `0x`, octal with a leading zero. It also accepts IPv6. That is right for a parser and wrong for a validator. Check the dotted-decimal shape first, then parse. Python's `ipaddress` module rejects leading zeros for this reason.

steps.prompt: Complete the pattern for one IPv4 octet, 0 to 255, with no leading zeros.
steps.explain: Read it from the top: 250-255, 200-249, 100-199, then 0-99, where `[1-9]?` allows an optional first digit that is not zero. The order matters little here, because the full pattern adds `\.` or the end after each octet.

steps.title: Parse a dotted IPv4 address, strictly
prompt: Write `IPAddress? ParseDottedIPv4(string s)`. Return the parsed address when `s` is exactly four decimal octets
0-255 separated by dots, with no leading zeros and nothing else; otherwise return `null`.
1. Check the shape with a regex. Anchor it with `^` and `\z`, not `$`: `$` also matches before a final newline, so
`"10.0.0.1\n"` would pass.
2. Then call `IPAddress.TryParse` to get the `IPAddress` object.
| input | result |
`System.Text.RegularExpressions` and `System.Net` are imported.
starter: return IPAddress.TryParse(s, out var ip) ? ip : null;
solution: return IPAddress.TryParse(s, out var ip) ? ip : null;
template: using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using System.Net;
{{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("10.0.0.1 parses", "10.0.0.1", ParseDottedIPv4("10.0.0.1")?.ToString());
Dojo.Eq("0.0.0.0 parses", "0.0.0.0", ParseDottedIPv4("0.0.0.0")?.ToString());
Dojo.Check("1 is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("1") is null, "IPAddress.TryParse reads it as 0.0.0.1");
Dojo.Check("0x7f.1 is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("0x7f.1") is null, "IPAddress.TryParse reads it as 127.0.0.1");
Dojo.Check("010.0.0.1 is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("010.0.0.1") is null, "a leading zero means octal to IPAddress.TryParse: 8.0.0.1");
Dojo.Check("256.1.1.1 is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("256.1.1.1") is null, "an octet is at most 255");
Dojo.Check("1.2.3 is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("1.2.3") is null, "exactly four octets");
Dojo.Check("1.2.3.4.5 is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("1.2.3.4.5") is null, "exactly four octets");
Dojo.Check("a trailing newline is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("10.0.0.1\n") is null, "end the pattern with \\z, not $");
Dojo.Check("an IPv6 address is rejected", ParseDottedIPv4("::1") is null, "only dotted IPv4");

require.message: Checks the shape with a Regex

hints: One octet is `(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|1[0-9]{2}|[1-9]?[0-9])`. The address is an octet, then `(\.octet){3}`.
`if (!Regex.IsMatch(s, @"^OCTET(\.OCTET){3}\z")) return null;` with OCTET written out, then `IPAddress.TryParse`.
